books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 2 (1840)

stimulus.text: “Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive.” — Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Volume 2 (1840).
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 2 (1840), Chapter 5. Verbatim quotation (Reeve translation), verified against the Bill of Rights Institute excerpts. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note

parts.prompt: Briefly identify what Tocqueville observed Americans doing.
parts.modelAnswer: Tocqueville observed that Americans of all ages and conditions constantly formed voluntary associations. They associated for every purpose, from business to religion to charity.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying Tocqueville's observation that Americans constantly formed voluntary associations.
scoring.notEarned: Restating the quotation with no identification of the observation does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way voluntary associations supported democracy in the 1830s.
parts.modelAnswer: Associations let ordinary people act together without waiting for government or a great lord. Democratic citizens learned to pursue common goals on their own.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one way associations supported democracy, such as letting ordinary people act together, building civic habits, or replacing aristocratic leadership.
scoring.notEarned: Saying associations were important without explaining how they supported democracy does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE limitation of Tocqueville's observation as evidence about American democracy.
parts.modelAnswer: Tocqueville visited for nine months and saw the free states most closely. His picture reflects the world of free white men more than the enslaved South or Native peoples.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one limitation, such as the short visit, the focus on free states and free white men, or the exclusion of enslaved people and Native peoples.
scoring.notEarned: Saying the observation is limited without naming what it leaves out does not earn the point.
